name: fig-02
title: fig-02: Orchestration
confidence_basis: Calibrated off Provisional (workbench 0.4.1). BASELINE (fig02-runnable): the fast/slow interleaving, sawtooth pool, and biomass staircase are robustly demonstrated — but its "cross-timescale mass conservation" (molecules + biomass == time) is actually a cumulative external-INPUT budget, not closed-system conservation; held at Medium. MECHANISTIC VARIANT (fig02-mechanistic, scientific-review revision): adds a stiff fast process + slow biomass with an explicit input-output ledger that closes to 1.8e-15 (and shows pool+biomass is NOT the budget), separates multirate scheduling from numerical accuracy (clean O(Δt) convergence of the stiff pool; fast-clock-controlled transient error), and verifies the scheduler is order-invariant. Held at Provisional overall because the rates/intervals are didactic and uncalibrated to a named metabolic timescale.
question: Is the paper's orchestration claim (Fig orchestration, panel a) executable rather than merely drawn -- does a runnable process-bigraph composite in which two processes update at DIFFERENT rates through ONE shared store actually reproduce multi-timescale coordination: the fast process filling the shared pool far more often than the slow one converts it, the two rates coordinated through the shared store, and the combined trajectory reflecting both timescales while conserving mass?
biological_summary:
This is the runnable realization of the paper's §Composition-vs-orchestration distinction (main.tex §composition vs orchestration; Fig orchestration, panel a). The paper defines orchestration as *when* processes act and *how* their updates are combined across timescales -- distinct from composition, which is *how* processes are coupled through shared variables. Panel (a) states it directly: "Multi-timescale orchestration coordinates processes that update at different rates through a shared store and discrete-event scheduling." (Panels (b) workflow-DAG and (c) event-driven graph rewrites are structural/schematic and are deliberately NOT part of this runnable demonstration -- only panel (a), the piece a minimal run can show honestly.)

The fig02-runnable composite (`meta_modelers_guide.composites.fig02-runnable`) wires two processes to one shared `pool` store, each on its own clock:
* `FastProduction` (interval 1.0, rate 1.0) adds to `pool.molecules` every base tick -- dmolecules/dt = +rate.
* `SlowConversion` (interval 5.0, yield_frac 0.6) fires once per 5 ticks, converting a fraction of whatever has accumulated in the pool into `pool.biomass` and drawing that same amount back out of `pool.molecules`.

Run together on the process-bigraph engine's discrete-event scheduler, the two clocks interleave and the combined trajectory reflects BOTH timescales: `molecules` ramps up on the fast clock (+1 per tick) and saws down each time the slow process fires, while `biomass` advances in a coarse staircase on the slow clock -- flat between slow firings, stepping up at each. Over the pinned 20-tick run the fast pool updates on every tick (20 changes) while the slow store changes only 3 times (the three visible conversions at t=10, 15, 20), so the fast process touches the shared store far more often than the slow one -- the multi-timescale signature made concrete. Crucially the two are coordinated through the ONE shared store and mass is conserved across the timescales: the fast process is the sole source and the slow process only MOVES mass between `molecules` and `biomass` within the pool, so at every emitted tick the shared-store total `molecules + biomass` equals the cumulative fast injection, which for rate=1.0 equals the elapsed time exactly (t=20: 8.12 + 11.88 = 20.0). The whole trajectory is deterministic -- no RNG anywhere -- so every number here reproduces exactly run to run.
claim: The paper's multi-timescale orchestration claim (Fig orchestration, panel a) is executable, not merely drawn: composing a fast process and a slow process through ONE shared `pool` store, each updating on its own interval, reproduces panel (a)'s "processes that update at different rates through a shared store" as a runnable, deterministic trajectory. Over a fixed 20-tick run the fast process updates the shared store on every tick (20 changes) while the slow process converts only 3 times, `molecules` is a sawtooth (rises on the fast clock, drawn down at each slow firing), `biomass` advances monotonically in a coarse staircase on the slow clock (levels 0 -> 3.0 -> 7.2 -> 11.88, never returning to the pool), and mass is conserved through the shared store across both timescales -- at every tick `molecules + biomass` equals the cumulative fast injection (== elapsed time), ending 8.12 + 11.88 = 20.0. The combined trajectory reflects both timescales at once; the composite is didactic and uncalibrated, so this demonstrates the ORCHESTRATION MECHANISM, not any biological magnitude.

variants.name: fig02-mechanistic
variants.rationale: Real-mechanism upgrade (scientific-review revision, Oct 2026). The baseline fig02-runnable shows the multirate signature but reports "molecules + biomass == elapsed time" AS IF it were mass conservation — it is actually a cumulative EXTERNAL-INPUT budget (influx 1/tick, no losses), the review's central objection. This variant builds a genuinely STIFF fast process (FastMetabolism: influx minus first-order turnover r·M, relaxing to the quasi-steady M*=I/r, so it truly needs a small timestep) sharing ONE pool with a SlowBiomass process on a long clock, and makes two things explicit the baseline conflated: (1) MULTIRATE SCHEDULING — which clock fires when; (2) NUMERICAL ACCURACY — convergence to a fine-step reference (clean O(Δt) in the stiff pool). The honest input-output ledger cumulative_input = ΔM + Δbiomass + Δwaste closes to 1e-15 every step, with waste (turnover + conversion loss) carrying most of the throughput — so pool+biomass is demonstrably NOT the budget. The baseline is kept intact as the didactic smoke test.

key_assumptions: This `fig02-runnable` composite is **didactic / toy-real**: a minimal illustrative demonstration built to make Fig orchestration panel (a) play forward under test, NOT calibrated to any literature. `FastProduction` (rate 1.0), `SlowConversion` (yield_frac 0.6), the intervals (1.0 and 5.0), and the 20-tick run length are hand-picked magnitudes chosen to make the two timescales legible in one short run, not fitted to any named biological process, rate, or measurement. The quantities `molecules` and `biomass` are abstract shared-store values, not calibrated concentrations or masses.

Only panel (a) -- multi-timestepping through a shared store -- is demonstrated at runtime. Panel (b) (workflow orchestration as a dependency DAG) and panel (c) (event-driven graph rewrites -- division, engulfment, bursting) are structural / schematic in the paper and are deliberately NOT part of this runnable composite. This study makes no runtime claim about (b) or (c).

The composite is fully deterministic -- there is no RNG in either process nor in the scheduler -- so every value pinned here (the final split, the biomass staircase levels, the shared-store conservation) reproduces exactly run to run. The exact numeric pins are regression pins over the current process configs and intervals; the directional claims (fast outpaces slow, sawtooth, monotone staircase, conservation) are the a-priori predictions that hold for any such fast/slow pair.

Orchestration timing here is the process-bigraph engine's own discrete-event scheduler acting on each process's declared `interval`. The slow process's effect becomes visible in the emitted `biomass` series one coarse step after each firing window; the ``interval`` fields, not any hand-written schedule, drive when each process acts.
acceptance_criteria: The fast process updates the shared store far more often than the slow process -- the two clocks are visibly different rates coordinated through one store.
The shared fast pool (`molecules`) is a sawtooth -- it rises on the fast clock and is drawn down each time the slow process fires -- so the combined trajectory reflects both timescales at once.
Biomass advances monotonically in coarse staircase steps on the slow clock and never returns to the pool -- the slow process moves mass one way, on its own clock.

Mass is conserved through the shared store across the two timescales -- the fast process is the sole source and the slow process only moves mass within the pool, so at every tick `molecules + biomass` equals the cumulative fast injection (== elapsed time). No mass is created or lost in crossing timescales.

units_and_time.time: 1 tick = 1.0 dimensionless base time unit (the fast process''s interval); the slow process fires every 5 such ticks; the run is 20 ticks.
units_and_time.quantities: `molecules` and `biomass` are dimensionless shared-store quantities (abstract pool amounts), not calibrated concentrations or masses. rate (1.0), yield_frac (0.6), and the intervals (1.0, 5.0) carry no physical unit.
units_and_time.note: No quantity here is calibrated to a named biological process, rate, or literature target; the magnitudes are didactic.

behavior_tests.name: mech-euler-convergence
behavior_tests.description: Refining the whole scheme (both clocks scaled together) converges to a fine-step reference: the stiff metabolite pool's L1 trajectory error falls monotonically toward zero, ~O(Δt) (first-order explicit Euler). Numerical ACCURACY is thus a distinct, measurable axis from multirate scheduling.

measure.expr: L1 pool error at integer times vs Δt, over Δt ∈ {1.0, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.0625}

pass_if.value: error falls monotonically and by >20× from coarsest to finest
pass_if.provenance: NUMERICAL_CONVERGENCE. Observed L1 pool error 2.27 → 0.10 → 0.052 → 0.025 → 0.011 as Δt halves (roughly slope-1 O(Δt)) (tests/test_fig02_mechanistic.py::test_euler_convergence_when_both_clocks_refined)

behavior_tests.name: mech-multirate-is-not-accuracy
behavior_tests.description: Multirate scheduling (which clock fires when) is NOT the same as numerical accuracy. The pool error is controlled by the FAST clock (the stiff turnover): with a coarse fast clock (r·Δt=1.5) the pool overshoots in the transient; refining only the fast clock cuts the error even at a fixed coarse slow clock. A coarse schedule can still be accurate if the stiff process is resolved on its own clock — the point of multirate.

measure.expr: |M(Δt_fast=1.0) − M_ref| vs |M(Δt_fast=0.1) − M_ref|, slow clock fixed

behavior_tests.name: mech-schedule-order-invariant
behavior_tests.description: Both processes read the shared pool at the tick boundary and return summed deltas, so coincident fast/slow updates are SYNCHRONOUS: swapping their order in the schedule leaves the trajectory identical to machine precision. findings.statement: The paper's multi-timescale orchestration claim (Fig orchestration, panel a) is executable: two processes updating at different rates through one shared pool store reproduce panel (a) as a runnable, deterministic trajectory. The fast process updates the shared store on every tick (20 changes) while the slow process converts only 3 times, so the fast clock visibly outpaces the slow one; molecules is a sawtooth (rises +1/tick, drawn down at each slow firing t=10, 15, 20) and biomass advances in a coarse monotone staircase on the slow clock (0 -> 3.0 -> 7.2 -> 11.88), so the combined trajectory reflects both timescales at once. All deterministic across repeated runs.

Nothing is created or lost in crossing timescales. This is the honest core of "combining updates across timescales": coordination through a shared variable that conserves what it holds. findings.statement: The cross-timescale conservation invariant holds at EVERY one of the 21 emitted ticks, not merely at the four sampled slow-firing landmarks: re-run in-memory, molecules + biomass == elapsed time to within 1e-9 for all ticks 0..20 (checked exhaustively, not spot-checked). Each slow firing converts exactly yield_frac (0.6) of the pool sampled at the start of its 5-tick window -- molecules at t=5, 10, 15 are 5.0, 7.0, 7.8, giving biomass increments 0.6x5.0=3.0, 0.6x7.0=4.2, 0.6x7.8=4.68 and the staircase levels [0.0, 3.0, 7.2, 11.88]. The invariant and the increment rule are therefore properties of the composition itself -- one source process plus one mass-moving process on a shared store -- not artifacts of where the series was sampled.

findings.statement: The baseline's "molecules + biomass == elapsed time" is a CUMULATIVE EXTERNAL-INPUT budget, not closed-system mass conservation — the mechanistic variant makes this explicit and honest. With a genuine first-order turnover routing mass to a waste sink, the full ledger cumulative_input = ΔpoolMetabolite + Δbiomass + Δwaste closes to 1.8e-15 on every step, while pool+biomass reaches only ~2.2 of the 20.0 input (waste carries ~17.8). So the quantity that "equals time" in the baseline is the input, not a conserved internal total; biomass is merely the yield-fraction of throughput.

findings.statement: Multirate SCHEDULING and numerical ACCURACY are distinct axes — the baseline conflated them. Refining the whole scheme converges in the stiff metabolite pool with L1 error 2.27→0.011 as Δt halves (~O(Δt), first-order Euler): accuracy is a measurable convergence property. Separately, the pool error is controlled by the FAST clock — a coarse fast clock (r·Δt=1.5) overshoots the quasi-steady pool in the transient while a fine fast clock tracks the reference, independent of the slow clock. That is exactly the value of multirate: a stiff process resolved on its own fast clock stays accurate even while a smooth process uses a coarse clock. The scheduler is also well-posed: swapping the process firing order leaves the trajectory identical (<1e-12), because both read the pool at the tick boundary and return summed, commuting deltas.

evidence.observed: L1 pool error 2.27→0.011 as Δt halves; fast-clock refinement cuts transient error; order-swap identical <1e-12

It grounds the paper's central figures-are-executable claim for the orchestration figure.

conclusion:
## Claims
- The paper's multi-timescale orchestration claim (Fig orchestration, panel a) is executable, not merely drawn: composing a fast process (interval 1.0) and a slow process (interval 5.0) through ONE shared pool store reproduces panel (a)'s "processes that update at different rates through a shared store" as a runnable, deterministic 20-tick trajectory. The fast process updates the shared store on every tick (20 changes) while the slow process converts only 3 times; molecules is a sawtooth (rises +1/tick, drawn down at each slow firing); biomass advances monotonically in a coarse staircase on the slow clock (0 -> 3.0 -> 7.2 -> 11.88), never returning to the pool.
- The two rates are coordinated through the one shared store and mass is conserved across the timescales: at every tick molecules + biomass equals the cumulative fast injection (== elapsed time), ending 8.12 + 11.88 = 20.0. The combined trajectory reflects both timescales at once, and nothing is created or lost in crossing them.

## Evidence
- **FAST-CLOCK-OUTPACES-SLOW-CLOCK** -- fast pool changes 20 times, slow store 3 times (20 > 3*3)
- **FAST-POOL-IS-A-SAWTOOTH** -- molecules rises +1/tick and drops at t=10, 15, 20
- **BIOMASS-ADVANCES-MONOTONICALLY-ON-SLOW-CLOCK** -- staircase 0 -> 3.0 -> 7.2 -> 11.88, monotone, exactly 3 conversions
- **MASS-CONSERVED-ACROSS-TIMESCALES** -- molecules + biomass == time at every tick; final 8.12 + 11.88 == 20.0
- **FAST-PROCESS-ADDS-EACH-TICK** -- unit control, +1.0 per unit interval
- **SLOW-CONVERSION-CONSERVES-WHAT-IT-MOVES** -- unit control, delta biomass + delta molecules == 0

## Limitations
- This composite is didactic / toy-real: the rates, yield fraction, intervals, and run length are hand-picked to make the two timescales legible, not calibrated to any biological process or literature target. It demonstrates the orchestration MECHANISM, not a biological magnitude.
- Only panel (a), multi-timestepping through a shared store, is demonstrated at runtime. Panels (b) workflow-DAG and (c) event-driven graph rewrites are structural / schematic in the paper and are not part of this runnable composite; this study makes no runtime claim about them.

## Next steps
- A future study could make panel (b) executable by wiring a small dependency DAG of Steps and asserting execution follows the dependency structure, and panel (c) by running an event-driven rewrite (division / engulfment / bursting) that mutates the composite structure mid-run.

It demonstrates the orchestration MECHANISM, not a biological magnitude.

Only panel (a) -- multi-timestepping through a shared store -- is demonstrated at runtime. Panel (b) (workflow orchestration as a dependency DAG) and panel (c) (event-driven graph rewrites -- division, engulfment, bursting) are structural / schematic in the paper and are deliberately NOT part of this runnable composite. This study makes no runtime claim about (b) or (c).

The exact numeric values pinned here (final split 8.12 + 11.88, biomass levels 3.0 / 7.2 / 11.88, the 20-vs-3 change counts) are regression pins over the current process configs and intervals; changing rate, yield_frac, or either interval would shift them. The DIRECTIONAL claims -- fast outpaces slow, sawtooth, monotone staircase, and conservation (molecules + biomass == elapsed time) -- are the robust, a-priori predictions that hold for any such fast/slow pair through one shared store.

This study is figure-only -- it has no calibrated spatial or biological cousin in the sibling `draft-to-living-cell` investigation. It stands as a minimal executable demonstration of the orchestration figure''s panel (a), not a scaled-up model.

Mechanistic variant (fig02-mechanistic) — scope and honest limits: it corrects the baseline's conservation overstatement (the ledger shows pool+biomass is only part of the input budget) and separates scheduling from accuracy, but it is still a 2-process linear ODE system integrated by explicit Euler on a 1-D abstract pool. The turnover/biomass rates, yields, and intervals are didactic (not a named metabolic timescale); the convergence is only first-order O(Δt); and panels (b) workflow-DAG and (c) event rewrites remain out of scope. "Waste" is an abstract loss sink, not a specified byproduct.
falsifiability: Overturned if the fast process does not update the shared store more often than the slow one, if molecules is not a sawtooth (missing either the fast fill or the slow draw-down), if biomass is not a non-decreasing coarse staircase on the slow clock, if the shared-store total (molecules + biomass) fails to equal the cumulative fast injection at any tick (implying mass created or lost across the timescales), or if any of these fails to reproduce exactly across repeated runs of the deterministic composite.

Baseline (didactic smoke test): the simpler pre-revision model of panel (a), multi-timestepping — two processes update at DIFFERENT rates through one shared pool. FastProduction (interval 1) fills molecules every tick while SlowConversion (interval 5) converts the pool to biomass in coarse staircase steps. Kept as the executable baseline; the mechanistic figure below adds the stiff dynamics, the scheduling-vs-accuracy distinction, and the honest ledger. From scripts/build_fig02_dynamics.py.

Mechanistic (the decisive figure): multirate orchestration that separates scheduling from accuracy. What to look for: (A) the update-EVENT RASTER — the fast metabolism process fires densely (Δt=0.25), the slow biomass process sparsely (Δt=1.0), through one shared pool; (B) the stiff metabolite pool (sawtooth) tracks a fine-step reference while the coarse-scheduled biomass staircase lags — SCHEDULING made visible; (C) the stiff-pool L1 error vs timestep falls ~O(Δt) — ACCURACY as a distinct, measurable convergence property; (D) the input-output LEDGER: cumulative input = pool + biomass + waste, where the waste sink (turnover + conversion loss) carries most of the throughput — so pool+biomass is NOT the budget, the honest replacement for the baseline's "pool+biomass==time". From scripts/build_fig02_mechanistic.py.

experiment: Run the `fig02-runnable` composite (FastProduction interval 1.0 rate 1.0 and SlowConversion interval 5.0 yield_frac 0.6 wired to one shared pool store) to completion over 20 ticks through the process-bigraph engine, and measure whether two processes updating at different rates through a single shared store reproduce Fig orchestration panel (a): the fast clock outpacing the slow clock, a sawtooth fast pool, a coarse monotone biomass staircase, and mass conserved through the shared store across the two timescales.
result: Over the deterministic 20-tick run, the fast process updates the shared store on every tick (20 changes) while the slow process converts only 3 times (at t=10, 15, 20), so the fast clock visibly outpaces the slow clock. `molecules` is a sawtooth -- it ramps +1/tick and is drawn down at each slow firing (9->7 at t=10, 11->7.8 at t=15, 11.8->8.12 at t=20) -- while `biomass` advances monotonically in a coarse staircase on the slow clock (0 -> 3.0 -> 7.2 -> 11.88), never returning to the pool. The two rates are coordinated through the ONE shared store and mass is conserved across the timescales: at every emitted tick `molecules + biomass` equals the cumulative fast injection (== elapsed time), ending 8.12 + 11.88 = 20.0. Every value is fixed and deterministic (no RNG), so the whole trajectory reproduces exactly run to run. The paper's multi-timescale orchestration claim (Fig orchestration, panel a) is thus executable, not merely drawn -- demonstrated here at the didactic (uncalibrated) level for the orchestration mechanism, with panels (b) workflow-DAG and (c) event rewrites left schematic.

biological_validation.basis: Reported in two layers, per the review. BEHAVIORAL (baseline fig02-runnable): the multirate signature runs — fast clock outpaces slow (20 vs 3 changes), sawtooth pool, coarse biomass staircase. BUT its "molecules + biomass == elapsed time" is a cumulative-input artefact, not conservation — behavioral verification, and the conservation phrasing was overstated. MECHANISTIC (variant fig02-mechanistic): the honest input-output ledger cumulative_input = ΔM + Δbiomass + Δwaste closes to 1.8e-15 with waste carrying most throughput (invariant); numerical accuracy is a measured O(Δt) convergence of the stiff pool, distinct from scheduling (numerical_convergence + mechanistic_ablation); and the scheduler is order-invariant (invariant). This supplies genuine mechanistic support for the orchestration claim and corrects the conservation overstatement. NOT biological calibration — the rates/intervals are didactic.

regression_compatibility.basis: fig02-runnable.composite.json builds and runs to completion through the process-bigraph engine over a deterministic 20-tick run (tests/test_fig02_runs.py, 7 tests); the two process handlers also pass unit-level controls driven directly. No optional heavy dependencies -- the demonstration is a minimal two-process composite.

explanatory_gain.basis: Making Fig orchestration panel (a) runnable -- rather than only drawn -- turns the paper's composition-vs-orchestration distinction into a checked fact: one can point to a live trajectory where two processes provably update at different rates through a shared store, the combined series carries both timescales, and mass is conserved across them. It grounds the paper's central figures-are-executable claim for the orchestration figure.
